```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
knitr::opts_chunk$set(fig.width = 10, fig.height = 6.5, dpi = 110, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)
```

The previous guides built [one network](from-references-to-networks.html)
and [found its clusters](finding-and-reading-clusters.html). A single
network of a long period, however, puts side by side literatures that
never coexisted, and hides how a literature is born, grows, splits or
fades. This guide follows the dynamic workflow that is the core of
networkflow: one network per time window, clusters in each window, and a
rule that links the clusters of successive windows into *dynamic
clusters* whose history can be told and drawn.

## One network per window

We build bibliographic coupling networks of the explanations of the
stagflation on sliding ten-year windows (1975-1984, 1976-1985...,
2004-2013), keep the main component of each, and detect clusters in each
window with Leiden.

```{r}
#| label: networks
library(networkflow)
library(ggplot2)
library(tidygraph)

nodes <- subset(Nodes_stagflation, source_type == "Stagflation")
networks <- build_dynamic_networks(
  nodes = nodes,
  directed_edges = Ref_stagflation,
  source_id = "source_id",
  target_id = "target_id",
  time_variable = "source_year",
  time_window = 10,
  window_step = 1,
  projection_method = "structured",
  cooccurrence_method = "coupling_similarity",
  edges_threshold = 1,
  filter_components = TRUE,
  verbose = FALSE
)
networks <- add_clusters(
  networks,
  clustering_method = "leiden",
  objective_function = "modularity",
  seed = 123,
  verbose = FALSE
)
n_window_clusters <- sum(sapply(networks, function(graph) {
  length(unique(as_tibble(graph, active = "nodes")$cluster_leiden))
}))
c(windows = length(networks), clusters = n_window_clusters)
```

Each window has its own clusters, numbered "01", "02"... These numbers
mean nothing across windows: cluster "01" of 1975-1984 and cluster "01" of
1976-1985 may be two different literatures.

## Linking clusters across windows

### The rule

`merge_dynamic_clusters()` links each cluster to a cluster of the
previous window when they share most of their documents. Let $V_a$ be the
documents of cluster $a$ in window $t-1$, and $V_b$ those of cluster $b$
in window $t$. Cluster $b$ inherits the identifier of $a$ when a majority
of $a$ goes to $b$ *and* a majority of $b$ comes from $a$:

$$
\frac{|V_a \cap V_b|}{D_a} > \tau
\quad \text{and} \quad
\frac{|V_a \cap V_b|}{D_b} > \tau,
$$

with $\tau$ the `threshold_similarity`, strictly above 0.5 so that each
cluster inherits at most one identifier and passes it to at most one
cluster. The denominators depend on `similarity_type`:

- `"complete"`: $D_a = |V_a|$ and $D_b = |V_b|$, all the documents of
  both clusters;
- `"partial"`: only the documents present in both windows count,
  $D_a = |V_a \cap V_t|$ and $D_b = |V_b \cap V_{t-1}|$.

With sliding windows, window $t$ loses the documents of the first year of
window $t-1$ and gains those of a new year. With `"complete"`, a cluster
that recruits many new documents, or loses many old ones, may lose its
identifier because its composition changed. With `"partial"`, only the
documents present in both windows are compared, and a cluster that
keeps its members together keeps its identifier however many documents
join it. The first view treats a cluster as a group of documents, the
second as a structure that recruits documents: which one fits depends on
the question.

The rule needs documents present in successive windows. With successive
windows (the default of `build_dynamic_networks()`), a network of documents shares no
document from one window to the next (each document has a single year),
and no cluster can be matched: sliding windows (`window_step = 1`) are necessary here.

```{r}
#| label: merge
window_networks <- networks # kept to compare other settings below
networks <- merge_dynamic_clusters(
  window_networks,
  cluster_id = "cluster_leiden",
  node_id = "source_id",
  threshold_similarity = 0.51,
  similarity_type = "partial"
)
```

### How sensitive are the dynamic clusters to the threshold?

The threshold and the type of similarity decide how easily clusters are
linked, hence how many dynamic clusters the history contains and how long
they live. `merge_diagnostics()` runs the matching for a grid of
thresholds and both similarity types, and `plot_merge_diagnostics()` draws
the result.

```{r}
#| label: thresholds
diagnostics <- merge_diagnostics(
  window_networks,
  cluster_id = "cluster_leiden",
  node_id = "source_id",
  thresholds = c(0.51, 0.55, 0.6, 0.65, 0.7, 0.75, 0.8, 0.9),
  min_length = 3,
  verbose = FALSE
)
diagnostics[diagnostics$similarity_type == "partial",
            c("threshold", "n_dynamic_clusters", "share_continued", "median_lifespan",
              "n_persistent", "share_nodes_persistent")]
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-diagnostics
#| fig-alt: >
#|   Four panels against the threshold, from 0.51 to 0.9, one line for
#|   complete and one for partial similarity. The number of dynamic clusters
#|   rises with the threshold, the share of window clusters with a
#|   predecessor, the median lifespan and the share of nodes in clusters of
#|   three windows or more fall; complete similarity is more sensitive.
plot_merge_diagnostics(diagnostics)
```

The `r n_window_clusters` window clusters become
`r diagnostics$n_dynamic_clusters[diagnostics$similarity_type == "complete" & diagnostics$threshold == 0.51]`
dynamic clusters at 0.51 and
`r diagnostics$n_dynamic_clusters[diagnostics$similarity_type == "complete" & diagnostics$threshold == 0.9]`
at 0.9 with the complete similarity
(`r diagnostics$n_dynamic_clusters[diagnostics$similarity_type == "partial" & diagnostics$threshold == 0.51]`
and
`r diagnostics$n_dynamic_clusters[diagnostics$similarity_type == "partial" & diagnostics$threshold == 0.9]`
with the partial one): the more demanding the threshold, the more clusters
are considered new. The curves are flat between 0.51 and 0.55, so that
values just above 0.5 are on a plateau: the continuities they produce do
not depend on the exact threshold. They bend after 0.55, and the second view
below shows what is lost. With the complete similarity, the median
lifespan falls to one window at 0.75: every window then has its own
clusters, which is the opposite of a history. The partial similarity is more
tolerant, because it ignores the documents that enter or leave the corpus
from one window to the next. This is the reason for the thresholds just
above 0.5 with partial similarity in the studies that used networkflow:
0.501 for @delcey2026, 0.55 for @duluins2026. Whatever the choice, the
continuities that a narrative relies on should survive close thresholds,
and a different seed of the clustering.

```{r}
#| label: fig-lifespans
#| fig-alt: >
#|   Stacked bars, one per threshold, for complete and partial similarity,
#|   showing the share of the nodes of all windows that belong to dynamic
#|   clusters living one window, two, three to five, six to ten, or more
#|   than ten. The share of one-window clusters grows with the threshold.
plot_merge_diagnostics(diagnostics, view = "lifespans")
```

The second view shows who pays for a high threshold: the nodes of long
clusters, which become members of short ones. With the complete similarity,
the clusters that live more than ten windows gather about half of the
nodes at 0.55 but 13% at 0.6, and none at 0.65: the longest continuities of
the history are cut into shorter pieces between 0.55 and 0.65. With the partial similarity, such clusters still
hold about 13% of the nodes at 0.9. The sensitivity of a continuity that
matters for the story, here between 0.55 and 0.6, is exactly what the
diagnostics are meant to reveal before it is hidden in a figure.

### Other ways to follow clusters

The rule of `merge_dynamic_clusters()` is simple and transparent, with
limits worth knowing. It compares a cluster only with the previous window,
so a cluster that vanishes for one window and comes back gets a new
identifier. Splits and merges are not recorded as such: the part that
meets the double majority keeps the identifier, the others are new
clusters. And the clusters of each window are detected independently,
which adds instability between windows. Other approaches exist, and
some could be tested on the same data:

| Approach | Idea | Compared with the double majority |
|---|---|---|
| Overlap matching with a Jaccard threshold [@greene2010] | Match the clusters of successive windows whose Jaccard similarity $\lvert V_a \cap V_b \rvert / \lvert V_a \cup V_b \rvert$ exceeds a threshold, and chain the matches into *dynamic communities*; splits and merges show up as one cluster matched to several. | Symmetric by construction, and gives a name to events; a one-to-one assignment (best match first) could replace the majority rule. |
| Multislice community detection [@mucha2010] | Detect communities in all windows at once, in a network where each node is tied to itself in adjacent windows with a coupling weight $\omega$. Identifiers are shared by construction. | The coupling $\omega$ plays the role of the threshold, but clusters of one window are influenced by the neighbouring windows: more stable, less independent. It needs nodes present in several windows (co-citation, authors, journals rather than documents). |
| Significance-clustered alluvial maps [@rosvall2010] | Bootstrap the network to find which clusters are robust, then draw the flows between robust clusters. | Addresses the instability of each partition rather than the matching rule; heavier. |

Two simpler checks are available with the tools of the package: running the
whole pipeline with several seeds of the clustering and comparing the
dynamic clusters with `merge_diagnostics()`, and varying the window and its
step (see the [first guide](from-references-to-networks.html)), since
instability often comes from windows that are too short to contain a
stable structure. Implementing the first two approaches in the package,
as alternatives to the double majority with the same output columns, would
allow comparing them on real corpora.

## Naming dynamic clusters

Once clusters are linked, each dynamic cluster can be named on all its
documents across windows (`name_merged_clusters = TRUE`), with the words of
the titles that distinguish it from the other dynamic clusters.

```{r}
#| label: names
networks <- name_clusters(
  networks,
  method = "tf-idf",
  name_merged_clusters = TRUE,
  cluster_id = "dynamic_cluster_leiden",
  text_columns = "source_title",
  nb_terms_label = 3,
  clean_word_method = "lemmatize"
)
```

## Drawing the history: alluvial plots

An alluvial plot shows the dynamic clusters as blocks in each window, with
a height proportional to their share of the window, and flows that follow
the documents from one window to the next. `networks_to_alluv()` stacks
the node tables into the long table such a plot needs, with statistics
on each cluster: its share of the whole history, its maximum share in a
window, and the number of windows where it exists.

```{r}
#| label: alluvial-table
alluv_dt <- networks_to_alluv(
  networks,
  intertemporal_cluster_column = "dynamic_cluster_leiden",
  node_id = "source_id"
)
cluster_stats <- unique(alluv_dt[, c("dynamic_cluster_leiden", "cluster_label",
                                     "share_cluster_max", "length_cluster")])
cluster_stats[order(-cluster_stats$length_cluster), ]
```

Clusters that exist in one or two windows, or remain small, clutter the
plot. We keep the clusters that last at least three windows, give each a
fixed colour, order the clusters to limit crossing flows
(`minimize_crossing = TRUE`) and place each label in the middle of the
cluster's life (`prepare_label = TRUE`).

```{r}
#| label: fig-alluvial
#| fig-height: 8
#| fig-alt: >
#|   Alluvial plot of the dynamic clusters of explanations of the
#|   stagflation, from the 1975-1984 window to the 2004-2013 window. Several
#|   clusters dominate the first windows and disappear in the late 1980s;
#|   three clusters appear in the 1990s and last until the end.
main_alluv <- alluv_dt[alluv_dt$length_cluster >= 3, ]
main_clusters <- sort(unique(main_alluv$dynamic_cluster_leiden))
palette <- data.frame(
  dynamic_cluster_leiden = main_clusters,
  color = scico::scico(length(main_clusters), palette = "batlow")
)
plot_alluvial(
  main_alluv,
  intertemporal_cluster_column = "dynamic_cluster_leiden",
  node_id = "source_id",
  color_alluvial = TRUE,
  color = palette,
  minimize_crossing = TRUE,
  prepare_label = TRUE,
  cluster_label_column = "cluster_label"
) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Share of the window") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
```

The plot draws the history that @goutsmedt2021 tells with qualitative and
quantitative methods. The early windows are shared between clusters on
wages, productivity, controls and unemployment, the explanations of the
late 1970s and early 1980s, centred on supply shocks and inflation
inertia. These clusters fade in the late 1980s, when windows contain few
documents. In the late 1980s and early 1990s, clusters on disinflation
and on time-consistent policy bridge the two periods. From the 1990s, new
clusters appear, on the "great inflation" and policy rules, on peacetime
inflation, and on oil prices and monetary alternatives, and last until the
end of the period: a new literature, centred on monetary policy, in which
the contributions of new classical economists, ignored by the first
explanations, became major references [@goutsmedt2021].

Reading the plot requires care. Flows between clusters are documents that
change cluster when the window slides, which may reflect a change in the
literature or simply the instability of a partition of a small network.
Windows of a dozen documents give fragile clusters: their part of the
plot should be read with the documents in hand.

## Coordinates that follow the documents

To draw the networks of successive windows side by side,
`layout_networks(compute_dynamic_coordinates = TRUE)` starts the layout of
each window from the coordinates of the previous one, so that a document
stays in the same region from one plot to the next. Giving the dynamic
clusters the same colours as in the alluvial (`color_networks()` with the
same palette) completes the picture: a cluster can be followed in the
alluvial and located in each network.

```{r}
#| label: dynamic-layout
#| eval: false
set.seed(1)
networks <- layout_networks(
  networks,
  node_id = "source_id",
  layout = "fr",
  compute_dynamic_coordinates = TRUE
)
networks <- color_networks(networks, column_to_color = "dynamic_cluster_leiden", color = palette)
```

## In research

The dynamic workflow was designed for histories of research fields, where
the question is less "what are the communities?" than "when did a
literature appear, what did it come from, and what did it become?".
@goutsmedt2023eer use bibliographic coupling and topic models to compare
the macroeconomics published in the *European Economic Review* with the
top five journals, between 1969 and 2002. @delcey2026 follow the
discussions of rationality in a corpus of nearly 260,000 economics
articles from 1900 to 2009. @duluins2026 apply the same tools to the
scientific reception of a report on the environmental impact of
livestock. In each case, the networks do not replace reading: they tell
the historian which documents to read, and which continuities and breaks
need an explanation.
